paras: The lynching of Pat Rhodes was the hanging of a wounded prisoner near Bayne's store, between New Madrid and Sikeston, Missouri, on the morning of May 12, 1881. Rhodes was one of four men accused of shooting into William Knox's house and killing a member of the posse sent after them. The wire said vigilantes hanged him, while local letters said only that he was found hanging in a stable while under guard.

A Sikeston letter to the Charleston Enterprise said Rhodes had spent the property of his wife, a widow named Knox, and was kept from her last farm by a Mr. Knox, after which he, James Hamilton, Myers and Brown "organized" to kill Knox and his family. The wire gave the motive as "an old grudge," and the Cairo Bulletin said Knox had exposed the men's secret organization. On Monday night, May 9 (Sunday, in one Memphis report), the four fired into Knox's house south of New Madrid; Knox escaped, but a man and a child were wounded.

Sheriff Walters (also spelled Waters) and a posse came upon the four near Bayne's store, where the men fired from behind logs in a thicket, killed Robert LaForge of New Madrid, wounded Albert Hunter and others, and took LaForge's watch, money and pistols. Rhodes, badly wounded, was left behind; he gave himself up at a woman's house, according to the Enterprise letter, or was found unable to travel and taken prisoner, according to the Cairo Bulletin.

He was kept under guard at Bayne's store. On Thursday morning he was found hanging in a stable nearby, at 11 o'clock by the Enterprise correspondent's account. The St. Louis Republican's Charleston special said a party of vigilantes took him out and hanged him, and the Memphis Public Ledger said "a crowd of vigilants hung him."

No report of an inquest into Rhodes's death, or of any arrest for it, appears in the coverage. Hundreds of men hunted the other three, who killed Sheriff John T. Davis of Wayne County before a citizens' party killed Hamilton and captured Myers, and Brown surrendered. Fearing a lynching at New Madrid, Sheriff Waters took the prisoners secretly to St. Louis.
Myers and Brown were tried at New Madrid in June for LaForge's murder, convicted, and hanged there on July 15, 1881, before about 5,000 people.

The Republican's special went out by telegraph on May 13 and ran that day in the Chicago Tribune, the Washington Evening Star and the Lancaster Intelligencer. Portland and Richmond papers carried it on May 14, and weeklies such as the Perrysburg Journal rewrote it a week later. Headlines used the word plainly: "Lynched by Vigilantes" in Chicago, "Mob Law" in Lancaster, and "Outrage, Desperadism, and Lynching" in Richmond. The wire called the four men "assassins" and "desperadoes" and reported the hanging in one sentence without comment.

Eastern weeklies reduced the story to a one-line item: "One of the desperadoes gave himself up and was lynched." A Wisconsin brief said Hunter had also been killed and that "a lynching will be in order at an early date" for the rest of the gang. The Princeton Union garbled the outcome, saying the outlaws were "shot dead or lynched" and later that the captured men were "hung by a mob."

The Missouri and Cairo letters did not use the word lynching. The Enterprise correspondent called the gang "remorseless banditti" with no parallel in "the jungles of Africa" and described Rhodes's death in euphemism. No account names the race of Rhodes, his companions or the men who hanged him.

The wire said vigilantes "took him out" and hanged him, the Enterprise letter said only that he was guarded until found hanging, and the Cairo Bulletin said he was kept under guard "until he escaped." Those two letters were written nearest the scene, but neither says who hanged him. The wounded at Knox's house also vary: Coleman and a child in the wire, a laborer, a woman and a child in the Enterprise letter, and George Williams and a girl who "died from wounds" in a county circular.

reader.title: Lynching of Pat Rhodes

bases: A wounded prisoner held under guard after a posse fight was hanged in a stable on May 12, 1881; the wire said a party of vigilantes took him out and hanged him (A1, A8, A12).

Rhodes was found hanged while held under guard, with no legal process, and the Charleston special and the Memphis Public Ledger said 'a party of vigilantes' or 'a crowd of vigilants' hanged him in reprisal for the attack on Knox's house and the killing of LaForge (A1, A8, A12); the local Enterprise and Cairo letters do not say who hanged him, and the Cairo letter says he had first escaped (A7).

The Charleston special, the Charleston Enterprise's Sikeston correspondent, the Cairo Bulletin letter and the county circular independently agree that the wounded Rhodes was taken prisoner and died by hanging (or 'died') on Thursday morning, May 12 (A1, A12, A7, A25); who hanged him rests on the wire account (A1, A8).

accounts.label: Wire report (St. Louis Republican's Charleston special)
accounts.gist: Rhodes, wounded by the posse, came in and gave himself up the evening of the fight; the next morning 'a party of vigilantes took him out and hanged him', and the others would be 'served in the same manner' if caught.

accounts.label: Sikeston correspondent of the Charleston Enterprise
accounts.gist: Rhodes gave himself up at a woman's house, was taken to Bayne's store and guarded until Thursday at 11, when he was found suspended in the stable nearby; the letter does not say who hanged him.

accounts.label: Cairo Bulletin letter
accounts.gist: The enlarged posse found Rhoades too badly wounded to travel and took him prisoner; he was kept under guard 'until he escaped' and was soon found hanging by the neck in a stable.

accounts.label: Memphis river news
accounts.gist: Rhodes surrendered and on Thursday morning 'a crowd of vigilants hung him'.

accounts.label: New Madrid county circular account
accounts.gist: Robert Rhoads was captured Wednesday evening, May 11, at J. D. Stepp's with five wounds and 'died Thursday morning'.

framing.detail: The Charleston special ran under 'Lynched by Vigilantes' (Chicago), 'Mob Law' (Lancaster) and 'Bloody Work in Missouri' (Washington), calling the men 'assassins' and 'desperadoes'.
The Richmond Dispatch headlined 'Outrage, Desperadism, and Lynching' and 'One of the Assassins Surrenders and is Lynched', putting the gang's crime first.
The Charleston Enterprise's correspondent called the gang 'remorseless banditti' worse than 'the jungles of Africa' and described the hanging only in euphemism, without naming who did it.
A brief in Wisconsin weeklies anticipated that 'a lynching will be in order at an early date' for the rest of the gang.
The Iron County Register reported matter-of-factly that the captured men 'would have been lynched ere this' had they stayed in New Madrid.
